output.text_basic:
Would you use a bike? Would you walk? Traveling by foot or bike would take a much longer time, especially now when we have been so used to getting across the city fast thanks to our vehicles.

But apart from the travel, think about the delivery of goods and services. If all cars stopped working, it would be catastrophic as the logistics and supply chain would be brought to a standstill. No more groceries, no more goods, and no more services. In fact, this would be a total disaster.

So, even though there's a push towards cleaner energy due to environmental concerns, it's important to have hybrid vehicles at least until we have a better alternative.

As you can already see, hybrid cars have advantages over fully electric and gasoline-powered cars. They are eco-friendly and more efficient, save you money, and provide a good balance between power and convenience.

As mentioned earlier, the technology is likely to get even more sophisticated in the years to come. Hybrid vehicles may one day become even more efficient, providing us with more ways to reduce our carbon footprint on the planet.

For the time being, when you are shopping for a new car, perhaps consider adding a hybrid vehicle to your shortlist. Not only will you be doing your bit for the environment, but you will also be saving a lot on fuel costs.

Your email address will not be published.
output.text_instructive: (Avoid common answers like walking, riding a bike, or using public transportation if they have been mentioned by others.)
output.text_cot:
First, it would take people a lot longer to move around, since cars can go up to 120-240 km/h, while the average human walking speed is 5km/h. Buses could take on a lot more passengers than cars, but with no cars on the road at all, it would be difficult to get buses everywhere needed in time. Bikes are a popular choice of transportation for many people for short distances, but they are less feasible for longer distances and difficult terrains. What's more, they also require infrastructure such as bike lanes which are not accessible everywhere.

So, with cars out of the picture, trains seem to be the most reliable and safest choice for long-distance travel. They don't require roads, can be powered by electrical energy (and therefore could even be solar or wind-powered), and they can take a lot of passengers at once, making them more space and energy-efficient than individual cars. 

Furthermore, in areas with harsh climates and terrain (think ice fields, deep valleys, or desserts), trains could be better equipped for such obstacles than cars. With more stable tracks and stronger axles allowing them to roll over rough terrain or slippery roads, trains would be less likely to get stuck or require costly infrastructure maintenance. 

Of course, we wouldn't be able to immediately switch to train travel as the preferred mode of transportation - it would take a lot of time and investment in building more train tracks all over the world to accommodate all the travelers previously using cars. 

Yet this begs the question: Why don't we invest more into train infrastructure now? Trains can be more energy-efficient and environmentally friendly than cars and planes, and if we dedicate more public funds and private investment to building and improving train networks, we could decrease our reliance on personal cars, which would in turn reduce carbon emissions and pollution, leading toward a more sustainable future. 

The next time you need to go somewhere - think twice about taking your car. Maybe there's a train nearby that could take you directly there, in style and with a smaller environmental footprint, all while sparing some space on increasingly crowded roads!

The future of sustainable transport may indeed be in electrified rolling stock, not in individual combustion engine-powered vehicles. Let's make this train of thought a reality.

A: During an EMP attack, many electronic devices would not survive, but people are not likely to be at risk from the pulse itself. The EMP energy would hit conductors such as wiring, metal pipes, telephone lines, etc. and create high currents which would likely burn out circuits or other electronic components that are not properly shielded against such an event. There's no evidence, however, that an EMP would directly harm humans. Concrete would not be a good choice for shielding since it is not a conductor. The safest places would be inside buildings made of conductive materials such as steel framing and metal siding. An all steel ship or submarine, or even an underground bunker with proper electrical grounding might offer excellent protection.

Note: The concern in many cases is not the EMP directly but the possibility of long-term loss of electricity and the services that depend on it. Would you know how to plant and grow fruits and vegetables? Would you know where to find edible plants in the wild? Learning these traditional survival skills is crucial for ensuring a future where you don’t have to depend solely on industry and agriculture to produce your food. Plus, it’s simply satisfying once you acquire a basic understanding of how these systems work.

Urban farming and gardening may become popular among a growing number of city dwellers. Cities around the world have begun the transformation by converting rooftops, vacant lots and unused spaces into productive gardens and farms. Not only does gardening provide food, but it also serves as a natural sanctuary where people can escape the urban hustle and bustle.

9. Alternative energy and housing

Imagine an energy system where you’re not restricted by blackouts, brownouts or fluctuations in energy rates. Renewable energy systems like solar panels, wind turbines and micro-hydro plants can provide reliable and sustainable energy without depleting resources or damaging the environment.

Housing may also shift towards sustainable and resourceful models. Architects around the globe are designing homes that integrate green designs and incorporate sustainable materials. These include earthships or homes built into the earth using tires filled with compacted soil, rammed earth walls, or simple designs of wooden structures combined with natural insulation. Additionally, housing that has the capability to generate its own energy using solar panels or wind turbines becomes not just a possibility, but a necessity.

10. Community living and cooperation

The breakdown of industrial society will force people to rely less on government and more on local communities. It’s easy to take for granted the complex networks of trade that ensure goods and services reach us. When that system falters, cooperation in local communities becomes essential for survival.

Learning to barter, trade and share resources with others in your local area is not just beneficial, but almost necessary in times of crisis. Small communities that can work together effectively will thrive when others fall. Hence, cultivating strong relationships with your neighbors and developing trust within your community now is far more valuable than you might think.

If you’re a like-minded individual, consider joining groups focused on sustainability, permaculture or preparedness. Sharing your skills and knowledge with others can create a support system you can rely on.

Where would you go? Where would you sleep? Where would you eat?

If your city were to disappear in a second, what would you do with the rest of your life? Where would you go? Who would you be with?

If the Earth itself and everything on it were to disappear, and you were somehow safe elsewhere, what would your next action be?

Would you try to find a new planet to call home, a new world to explore, a distant star to orbit?

Would you remember where you came from? Would you tell stories about the strange creatures, the incredible plants, the oceans, mountains, skyscrapers?

Would you grieve? Would you mourn?

Maybe you would focus on survival: adapting to the new environment, finding a sustainable source of food, creating shelter and clothing.

We could do all of those things—and more.

But let me propose another possibility.

Imagine, in all of your future travels, you suddenly encounter another human being. Perhaps they have been in exactly the same situation as you: suddenly swept up from Earth and set adrift.

What would be the first thing you would want to do?

Would you seek to protect yourself, make sure this other person isn't a threat?

Would you be curious about them? What stories could they tell from the vanished Earth?

Or would you be desperate for connection? Would you yearn to hear your native language, to laugh together, to embrace each other?

If you are anything like me, you would treasure that encounter, that unexpected glimpse of home. You would cling to it.

Humans are social animals. We evolved to stick together, watch each other's backs, care for the young, help the wounded. We have an inbuilt need to feel connected to others.

We can find that connection in family, in friendships, in communities. We can foster it through shared rituals, storytelling, art, play.

Connection isn't always easy. It requires effort, vulnerability. It's messy. But when it goes well, it is deeply satisfying. It makes life more vivid.

It matters.

However, it's advisable to consider that different purification methods work best for different types of pollutants. Below are some methods of purifying dirty river water before drinking.

    1. Ultraviolet Purification

Ultraviolet purification is a non-chemical method where UV light penetrates the water and kills the microorganisms like bacteria, cysts, and viruses responsible for the diseases. It also destroys the DNA of these microorganisms, essentially inactivating them. Ultraviolet purifiers are effective and easy to use. The UV light does not remove sediments, particles, and chemicals from the water. Hence, for better results, it's advisable to use a proper water filter or a purifier to eliminate contaminants (chemicals and particles) before UV treatment.

    1. Boiling

Boiling is one of the oldest and most common methods of purifying dirty water. This process works by killing microorganisms such as bacteria, viruses, and parasites that make the water unsafe for drinking. To ensure all contaminants are dead, boil the water at a rolling boil for about one minute. Then, let it cool down before drinking.

Although boiling is incredibly efficient, it does not remove chemicals, heavy metals, and particulates that might be present in some water sources. Therefore, it's ideal to use this method in conjunction with a water filter or an activated carbon filter.

    1. Filtration

Water filtration is another effective method of purifying dirty river water, making it safe for drinking. When you pass the water through a filter, several contaminants like dirt, suspended particles, bacteria, and protozoa get trapped or blocked, leaving you with clean and safe drinking water.

The filtration process can be done through a variety of methods:

        • Ceramic filters: These use a ceramic material with fine pores to trap pathogens and other water contaminants. Ceramic filters are environmentally friendly to use and don't require electricity.
        • Hollow fiber filters: These are advanced filters made from synthetic fiber strands arranged in a tight arrangement. They have a high surface area and tiny pores that trap bacteria, viruses, and other contaminants as water passes through them.
        • Charcoal filters: Activated charcoal filters use a layer of carbon to remove contaminants through adsorption, a process where impurities are attracted to the surface of the carbon filter.

I imagine there would still be ways to protect yourself from fire or cold, like moving your campsite with the sun or building a shelter out of the natural environment (or finding old ones). However, the question asks specifically about covering the body with fabric.

Covering the body with large leaves, animal skin, or something similar could provide basic protection, but would it offer substantial protection against the elements (cold, heat, wind, rain)?

Are there any recorded examples of people doing this?


Historically, the Inuit constructed anoraks from caribou or seal skin. These garments offered excellent thermal insulation from the cold. If you look at the clothing worn by the indigenous peoples of the Americas and Arctic regions, they feature skins and furs as the primary materials, rather than textile from plant fibers. These materials are inherently waterproof, and the fur can also provide insulation.

Leather on the other hand, would not provide any significant insulation. However, it could be a component in a layered garment.

As far as I'm aware, no historical culture relied solely on plant-based textiles (fabric) for protection from the elements.

Solar ovens are a fantastic emergency preparedness tool. In this article we’ll look at how they work and why each emergency preparedness kit should include one.

How Do Solar Ovens Work?

Solar ovens reflect and concentrate sunlight to convert it into heat. Most designs have three parts: A reflective material (usually polished aluminum), a cooking pot and an insulating material (often polycarbonate).

The reflective material is shaped to focus sunlight onto the pot from all angles, creating a small, intensely hot area. The cooking pot is made of dark, heat-conductive material and is insulated against heat loss to the air. Finally, the insulating bag or box prevents heat from escaping the pot, ensuring that it remains hot even after the sun goes down.

Solar Ovens: Top 5 Benefits

1. Safe

Solar ovens are safe to use indoors (provided that the room is well-ventilated). If you’re concerned about the risks of starting cooking fires or damaging property, solar ovens pose no threats. They can also be used to pasteurize water: Heating water to 150°F (66°C) is usually enough to kill most pathogens without boiling it. 

2. Cost-Effective

Compared to other non-electric cooking methods, solar ovens have minimal operational costs. Once you have the initial kit, they can be used indefinitely. There are no fuels to buy, no electricity costs and no gas bills.

3. Low Impact

Unlike traditional and portable cooking solutions, solar ovens have a low environmental impact. They don’t produce pollutants and don’t contribute to deforestation. They’re also lightweight and mobile, perfect for evacuating or bugging out.

4. Multiple Uses

While solar ovens are often used for cooking meals, they also have multiple utility purposes in a survival context. They can be used for baking, heating soup, frying and boiling water. Some models can reach temperatures sufficient for preserving foods.

5. Convenience

Solar ovens can be a great choice for outdoor cooking under favorable conditions. On a clear, sunny day, you can cook a meal without having to be present throughout the process.

Once you've chosen a fuel source, evaluate your heating options.

Active Heating Systems

Active heating systems require a power source: either electricity or fuel.

Electric heating systems are convenient and practical for grid-tied homes, since they integrate well with furnaces, baseboards, and space heaters. But if the power goes out, you're out of luck!

Fuel-powered systems include furnaces, boilers, and hot water-based heat.

Passive Heating Systems

Passive heating systems rely on the principles of architecture, home design, and insulation. They are ideal for off-the-grid living since they require little maintenance and no active heating source.

Solar gain: Building a south-facing home or adding south-facing windows will allow the sun to heat your home, especially if you use interior walls made of thermal mass materials like concrete or bricks.

If the servers were to crash (and if your Wi-Fi router still works), what sort of information would be available? None. Living without internet, smartphones and other gadgets is a possibility, and it comes with its own set of pros and cons.

Living Technology-Free

How would you feel if you gave up the internet and your smartphone forever? Would it be hard for you to adapt or would it be a walk in the park? A man named Richard Perkins decided to give up the internet, something he depended on heavily for his work, after he realized how much of his life he spent staring at screens. In today's world, living without technology is quite the challenge. However, there are people out there who have found ways to do it. The Amish are one such group. They reject most forms of modern technology, which includes automobiles, air conditioning, and home computers. They live simple lives, choosing to focus on strong family bonds, community and connection with nature. This decision is influenced by their religion and they believe that such a way of living brings them closer to their faith. As a result, Amish people typically live longer and display lower depression rates compared to non-Amish individuals.

Better Sleep: The blue light emitted from smartphones, computers and other gadgets can disrupt sleep patterns.

output.text_basic:
Using stairs, silly! Of course, this assumes that the skyscraper is accessible by stairs in the first place, which isn't always the case. But let's set that aside for now. If you had to use the stairs to get to the top of a skyscraper, how long would it take you?

According to The Telegraph, a journalist for the newspaper attempted this very experiment, climbing the 1,792 steps it takes to get to the top of Chicago's Willis Tower (formerly the Sears Tower). He completed the climb in just under two hours, which means he climbed at a rate of about 32.4 steps per minute. Most people don't climb stairs that quickly, especially if you're also talking, taking photos, and getting the word out on social media like the reporter was.

Assuming a more leisurely pace of 20 steps per minute, which according to the University of Iowa is average for most fit adults (though it declines with age), it would take someone approximately 89.6 minutes to climb up 1,792 stairs, or about 1 hour and 29.6 minutes. If you're looking to reach the roof of something the size of Willis Tower, be prepared for a significant physical challenge, especially considering that this doesn't factor in the possibility of taking breaks or dealing with fatigue.

How to plan for stairs for disabled and elderly people

Even buildings designed for ADA compliance that include an elevator still need to have a means of egress for people with disabilities in case of emergencies, meaning they need accessible ways to navigate the stairs (via ADA National Network). To accommodate such needs, building codes often include requirements for wheelchair lifts or ramps, along with handrails, non-slippery stair nosings, and appropriate fire-protection systems.

Even in new construction, it can be challenging to create truly accessible means of egress for people who use wheelchairs or have other mobility issues. Many factors come into play, including the building's design, space constraints, and budget. However, with proper design and thoughtful planning, it's possible to create a building that is accessible for everyone. That way, in the unlikely event that an elevator ceases to function, everyone would have a means to safely exit the building or get to their destination through the building's interior stair wells.

I asked this question of a few folks recently and got answers like “open windows,” “fans,” “sunlight,” and “do nothing” (a common response when it comes to not using energy).

Even with our modern conveniences, our ancestors were experts at staying warm and cool without electricity. Today, the traditional techniques hold lessons for those interested in saving energy.

The following methods can be used separately or in combination to maintain a comfortable temperature for a home or room.

1. Location, Location, Location. This is the number one rule of maintaining a comfortable temperature. The orientation of the building on the property can help it take advantage of the natural elements. Trees can block harsh summer sun or biting winter winds.

2. Cross Ventilation. Many older homes have windows on opposite sides of a room or the house allowing air to flow through when both windows are open.

3. Thermal Mass. Thick walls and ceramic tile floors can store up heat during the day from the sun shining through windows and release it at night when temperatures drop.

4. Ceiling Fans. These increase air speed, which makes a room feel cooler. In the winter, fans can be reversed to draw the warmer air, which rises to the ceiling, back down into the room.

5. Radiant barriers. Aluminum foil is an effective radiant barrier. It can be used in attics to block the summer heat or inside windows to reflect room heat back into the room during the winter.

6. Heavy Curtain. Close thick curtains during the heat of the day to block the sun or open them to let in sunlight to warm the house in winter.

7. Insulation. This is a modern material that is used to resist heat flow. It could be down comforters on beds, extra clothing, or blow-in insulation in attics.

8. Sunrooms and solariums can serve as mini greenhouses, allowing the sun to warm up the space during the day and trapping this heat.

9. Transpiration and vegetation. Trees and large plants release water vapor, which can cool the surrounding air. Plantings can also block sun or wind.

10. Earth sheltering or berms, which use the natural insulating properties of the earth.

11. Fireplaces, whether gas or wood-burning, can provide warmth.

12. Natural building materials, including clay, cob, and straw bales, can also help insulate a building and maintain comfortable temperatures.

13. Skylights can be used as a natural source of heat and light in the winter.

14. High ceilings.

Ancient people used clay or stone slabs to record information. Later, they found a way to write on other materials, like leather and silk. But paper provided a lot of benefits like being lightweight and very cheap.

A Chinese official named Ts’ai Lun is traditionally credited with inventing paper in 105 CE. He figured out that if he pounded bark, hemp, rags, and fish nets into a pulp and pressed the pulp flat, he could then dry the fibers into sheets. This material became known as paper.

In the centuries that followed, paper was made from many different materials, and each region added their own modifications. The Arabs made their paper from linen and used it for writing and bookmaking as early as the 8th century.

In China, it wasn’t until about the 13th century that paper became widespread. Paper money, playing cards, and even toilet paper came into use in China around this time. Before then, people had to rely on more… natural and less comfortable methods to manage their bodily needs.

Paper money’s origins can be tied to China. The first known paper banknotes were used in the Tang Dynasty. They were actually receipts that could be traded for goods.

As for toilet paper, the Chinese reportedly used it as early as the 6th century. They made their toilet paper from de-inked and scented rice straw. Much later, in 1393, the Chinese emperor ordered that ten thousand sheets of two foot square toilet paper to be made for imperial family use.

In Japan, the Kojiki, which is one of the oldest books compiled as early as 712 CE, was printed on paper made from the mulberry plant. Mulberry paper played a significant role in the religious culture of the Far East.

The papermaking industry spread from China to Korea to Arabia and then to Europe. By the 15th century, water-powered mills were used in Spain, Italy, Germany, and other parts of Europe, and papermaking had become an industry.

Your body has its own built-in clock, and here are some of the things we know about it. The human body clock runs on a 25-hour day but it has to squeeze itself into a 24-hour day. To fit in, the clock has to adjust by an hour every day.

Your body clock uses light to set itself. It is programmed to respond most strongly to blue light which is most prevalent just after dawn.

The body clock consists of about 20,000 nerve cells that make and release a protein called PER. Levels of PER build up in each nerve cell during the night, then fall during the day, taking roughly 24 hours to complete the cycle. The cells work as a group to keep the cycle on track.

The cycle of PER building up and breaking down influences many other cells in the body. Hormones flood the body at certain times of day, core body temperature rises and falls and performance peaks and troughs.

For example, levels of the hormone melatonin, sometimes dubbed the 'Dracula of hormones' because it scurries away from daylight, rise rapidly after dusk. They stay high all night, signalling to the body that it's time to sleep.

A body clock out of sync with the outside world can have serious health consequences. Nightshift workers are at greater risk of obesity, diabetes and heart disease. This disruption of the rhythm may be linked to higher levels of stress hormones, imbalances in glucose and insulin levels and changes in the timing of when the body expects to eat.

Research indicates that teenagers may have a natural body clock that goes to bed later and gets up later than adults. This has implications for school timetables as some experts argue that early starts mean teenagers miss out on sleep and learn less.

Scientists studying body clocks are hopeful that they can use this research to improve health. In particular, there's a hope that drugs could reset the body clocks of people with jet lag, shift work or sleep disorders.

For example, UK researchers think it might be possible to develop a slow-release drug that would damp down or boost PER levels, effectively rewinding or fast-forwarding time inside the body.

output.text_basic:
If you had a large water storage tank that you filled in the spring, you could use this stored water to irrigate your garden.

Cisterns are man-made water storage tanks that have been used for hundreds of years to store rainwater. The rain would be collected from the roof during a rainstorm and directed into the cistern through a gutter and downspout system.

An essential part of a cistern system is the water purification steps. The water from the roof could be quite dirty and full of undesirable particles.

The collected water usually first enters a pre-filter that would remove large floating debris such as leaves or sticks. Then, the water would typically pass through a fabric filter to remove even smaller particles.

Activated charcoal is usually the final element in a complete filter system. Charcoal will remove particles down to a size of 0.5 microns and also serve to remove microorganisms and chemicals.

Historically, water treatment would stop with charcoal filtration. But modern techniques can go further. Ultraviolet sterilization and additional chemical treatments may be beneficial depending on the local situation.

A complete water treatment system will ensure that the stored water is safe for human consumption as well as for your vegetable garden.

Modern cistern systems incorporate numerous innovations to simplify installation and maintenance.

For example, a header tank at the top provides the pressure needed for indoor plumbing. And an overflow system prevents overfilling and damage to your home in case of particularly heavy rainfall.

One of the biggest advantages of a cistern system is that it can be virtually independent from public utilities. If the city water supply fails, or if water costs become prohibitively high, cistern water remains available for your family’s needs.

Rainwater is also soft water, which means fewer problems with mineral buildup in plumbing fixtures and water heaters.

Another huge advantage of using rainwater in your garden is that you are using a free, sustainable resource that does not deplete wells or aquifers.

On its journey to your roof, rainwater will wash various airborne particles, including nitrogen and sulfur compounds. Small amounts of these compounds in rainwater can be beneficial nutrients for your plants.

However, you must also be cognizant of potential pollutants. If your roof has been treated with chemicals (especially copper-based algaecides), these toxins could leach back into the rainwater.

For a small backyard garden, a barrel or drums can suffice to collect rainwater. But for a productive market garden, you might consider a larger system.

Life would be very different. Imagine having to back up into a parking space every time or shuffle backwards through your house to avoid obstacles.

Yet this is the world people with Friedreich's ataxia (FA) inhabit, a rare genetic disorder that strikes in childhood and gradually robs the body of its ability to move as muscles weaken and waste away.

FA is named after Nikolaus Friedreich, the German physician who first described the disorder in the 1860s. It's caused when a defect in the gene frataxin results in a deficiency of the protein that it produces. Though researchers don't yet understand the exact role of frataxin, they suspect it plays some part in protecting mitochondria, the cell's energy-producing powerhouses, from wear and tear.

FA is marked by muscle weakness and stiffness, loss of balance, and impaired sensory perception. But the movement problems are only part of what makes life difficult for people with FA. Since frataxin is important in many of the body's organs, a range of other symptoms arise: heart defects, diabetes, scoliosis (curvature of the spine), and hearing and vision loss.

Because walking canes, walkers, and wheelchairs can't provide complete mobility, new approaches are needed to help people with FA move.

The idea behind the reverse walker is simple: When a person with Friedreich's ataxia steps into it, the walker takes over, propelling the person backward.

"The reverse walker provides freedom by eliminating the need for assistance from a caregiver while moving," said inventor Sarpoma S. Patil, an engineering professor at Worcester Polytechnic Institute (WPI) in Worcester, Massachusetts. "The device is the first-of-its-kind, and we believe it will be beneficial to patients worldwide."

Patil said the inspiration for the reverse walker stemmed from his work mentoring a team of undergraduate students participating in WPI's Entrepreneurship Minor, a program that encourages students to apply knowledge and skills from multiple disciplines to creating innovative products.

The students heard about FA and brainstormed ideas with a physical therapist who treats Friedreich's ataxia patients. They explored the idea of a mobility aid that would allow a person with limited leg strength and balance to move around independently.

Reverse Walking

The result is a walker with a twist: It moves in reverse. "Reverse stepping is more natural for ataxia patients, and it doesn't require complex foot-switch mechanisms to control the direction of movement," said Patil.

The walker is driven by two electric motors

Another way to increase voltage is by using DC to DC converters. These are more complicated circuits designed to convert lower DC voltage to higher DC voltage. Usually, larger devices use switch mode power supply instead of relying on battery voltage for power.

Another case is when you have batteries delivering higher voltage than needed by the device. Here you have few options. You could just connect your device directly to batteries, adding some kind of current limiting, if necessary. Or you could use a voltage divider to lower the voltage before it enters your device. Voltage divider is usually simple resistor network with two or more resistors connected in series.

There are hundreds of ways how you could use batteries and devices with different voltage requirements, above are just few most common examples.

Frottage has its roots in art that began in the 1930s. Artists found they could make pictures by rubbing paper on textured surfaces, like walls. They'd then either ink or color the transferred designs.

Some frottage artists use plants to rub onto paper instead of inking the designs. This is known as plant rubbing or nature printing. It can create richly detailed designs of tree bark, leaves, flowers, grasses, and even vines.

To practice frottage with plants, be prepared outside. You’ll need:

  • fresh, sturdy plant leaves or grasses, or thin branches
  • white drawing paper (heavier paper will work better)
  • a cardboard or heavy paper “sandwich" (a piece of cardboard that's slightly bigger than the paper and cut to fit inside the paper as a backing)
  • scissors
  • clipboard

Here’s what to do:

1. Look at the natural world around you. Choose a leaf, blade of grass, or branch with an interesting texture that you would like to capture in your artwork.

2. Cut the cardboard or heavyweight paper slightly larger than the drawing paper to place inside the drawing paper. It acts as a support for the paper.

3. Place a piece of white drawing paper on the cardboard or paper “sandwich.”

4. Place the plant you’ve chosen on top of the paper. Arrange it so you can see through the leaf, grass, or branches onto the paper.

5. Place a thin, even layer of newspapers over the plant. This will protect the plant.

6. Smooth your hand over the newspapers to apply pressure. You want the plant’s texture to be transferred to the paper underneath.

10. Consider using the plant as a stamp. Dip it in paint and then stamp it onto a larger area of paper.

Without the ability to taste food, mealtime becomes less enjoyable and eating less satisfying. When you get a cold or sinus infection, it's common to temporarily lose your sense of taste. But if you've lost your sense of taste and it's not because of a temporary illness, what could be causing this problem—and more importantly, can it be fixed?

What Causes Loss of Taste?

Taste disorders have many possible causes, and determining the exact cause can take time. Here are several factors that can cause a loss of taste:

1. Upper Respiratory Infections

Sinus infections, colds, and other upper respiratory infections can lead to taste disturbances. This is generally due to nasal congestion that disrupts airflow to the nose. Your sense of smell plays a major role in what you taste, so when your nose is stuffy, flavors become dull.


Ear infections can also affect your sense of taste. The Eustachian tube—which connects your ear to your throat—can become clogged with fluid during an ear infection and cause taste disturbances.

3. Oral Health Conditions

Gum disease, mouth infections, and other oral health conditions can affect taste. Certain mouthwashes, toothpaste, and dental procedures may also alter taste.

4. Nutritional Deficiencies

Low levels of zinc, vitamin B12, and iron can lead to taste disturbances. Not eating a balanced diet, certain medical conditions like digestive disorders, or not absorbing nutrients properly can contribute to these deficiencies.

5. Neurological Conditions

Injuries, tumors, or diseases affecting the head and brain—including the nerves related to taste—can lead to impaired taste. These can include brain injuries, Alzheimer’s disease, or stroke.

6. Medications

Many prescription and over-the-counter drugs can alter taste. Drugs that can cause this include:

  • Antibiotics like amoxicillin
  • Antihistamines and decongestants
  • Antidepressants
  • Antacids
  • Certain cardiovascular drugs

7. Exposure to Certain Substances

Exposure to certain chemicals, such as insecticides and solvents, may also affect taste.

8. Aging

As people age, they gradually lose taste buds, though most older adults still maintain enough to detect flavors.

9. Nervous System Disorders

Conditions such as multiple sclerosis or Bell’s palsy may influence taste.

10. Other Causes

Cigarette smoking, fungal infections, nasal polyps, and endocrine disorders can also contribute to impaired taste.

Diagnosing a Taste Disorder

Many people say that we generate more waste now than ever before. But there was a time when waste management didn’t exist, and people had to be more creative and mindful about what they threw away.

Here is an example: What might have happened to the leftovers from Thanksgiving dinner in 15th-century England? 

Let’s explore a few hypothetical scenarios:

  1. A peasant: With limited resources, a peasant likely relied on pigs or other livestock to help dispose of food waste and bones. They might have fed scraps to their chickens and dogs, too. Food waste that didn’t feed animals was likely tossed onto a compost pile in a designated area of their property.
  1. A lord or noble: The wealthy often hosted lavish, multi-day dinners and feasts, generating large amounts of waste. In these instances, leftovers could have been given to the poor who lined the roads of the castle, or food waste could have been fed to livestock. Sturdy food scraps like fruits and vegetables, or bones, may have been preserved into jams or saved for soup stock. Anything still edible would have been packed up and distributed to the less fortunate in town.

What would you have done?

Without much modern technology or waste management infrastructure, ancient civilizations had to think creatively about how to handle their trash. Many ancient people practiced a form of recycling or repurposing out of necessity—for example, using animal skins for clothing, turning food waste into compost, or repurposing wood and metal.

In modern times, we have luxury of waste management companies that pick up our trash and dispose of it properly. We have recycling programs and options for composting food scraps.

But what would YOU do if you had no waste bin and nowhere to throw your trash? How would you adapt to this kind of challenge?

Lastly, collect your important documents, valuables, and family heirlooms and keep them in a fireproof safe, preferably in your car, if you can still safely access it.

These are the questions many parents face when they homeschool. But before you dismiss homeschooling entirely, let's explore what it's all about—starting with the benefits of homeschooling.

Why Do People Choose to Homeschool?

People choose to homeschool for a variety of reasons. Some families make the decision based on philosophical beliefs, religious convictions, or educational methods they believe are best for their children.

Other families might decide to homeschool if:

  • Their children are struggling in school due to learning disabilities.
  • They believe the local school system isn't providing a high-quality education.
  • They have strong personal beliefs and values that they want to pass on to their children without interference.

Some students might have unique interests that can't be fully explored in a traditional classroom setting.

Regardless of why a family chooses to homeschool, the educational outcome depends largely on parental engagement and motivation as well as the student's willingness to learn.

Is Homeschooling Good for the Child?

Homeschoolers tend to have good academic records and positive attitudes about learning. A 2009 study by the U.S. Department of Education found that homeschooled students typically scored above average compared to their peers who attend public or private school.

Some advantages of homeschooling include:

  • Greater parental involvement, which has been shown to have a more profound effect on academic achievement than the type of school.
  • Flexibility in curriculum and environment that can support a student's learning style and needs.
  • Freedom to pursue interests and develop talents, a skill set vital to future successes.
  • A more nurturing environment where students can develop at their own pace.
  • Exposure to a wide range of topics and experiences, rather than a narrowly focused school curriculum.

Are there any downsides to homeschooling?

Concerns about Socialization

One of the most common criticisms of homeschooling is that children who are taught at home might not have enough interaction with peers, which they need to develop social skills.

While this might have been a valid argument in the past, the growing number of homeschooling families means there are increasing opportunities for children to engage with other kids. There are homeschool co-ops and social clubs, sporting groups, and community activities where homeschooled children can meet and interact with their peers.

Think about this. What if a local currency like the Brixton Pound popped up to replace the Pound Sterling? Could this really work? In this article, we look at the mechanics of local currency schemes to see how they fit into the mainstream economy.

Local currencies and the mainstream economy

The idea of a local currency is not new. It goes back to the 1930s when many towns across the Great Plains of America suffered a series of bank failures and could no longer access central money. In response, local businesses began printing their own money, essentially IOUs, to facilitate business transactions. The local Chamber of Commerce would vouch for these IOUs and the money became widely accepted.

There have been numerous other examples of local currencies from around the world. In recent times there has been a resurgence of interest in community currencies as a way of encouraging people to buy local goods and services and build stronger local economies. The Transition Towns network, for example, supports the development of local currencies as a way of keeping wealth within communities.

The Brixton Pound is an initiative of the Brixton Pound project (run by Brixton Credit Union) and the local traders who accept the currency. Its aim is to stimulate the local economy by encouraging people to shop locally. The local businesses display the B£ sign in their windows to show that they accept Brixton Pounds. This sign is a form of advert for the local traders too, as it shows locals and visitors to Brixton that their goods and services are locally sourced.

How does local currency work?

Local currencies work alongside the national currency and can be exchanged in two main ways: directly and through local banks.

Direct schemes are the original and simplest form of local currency. They work like vouchers or coupons whereby notes are issued to traders who have goods and services to sell. For example, ten £1 notes will be issued for a £10 transaction between two traders. These notes then circulate between businesses when purchasing resources that are locally available. In a direct scheme, there is always a one-to-one, pound-for-pound relationship between the local currency and the national currency.

Currency linked schemes, like the Brixton Pound, are slightly different in that they aim to provide a longer term solution for local businesses. Local traders can receive a bank account in B£. They can then spend this in B£ shops and receive payment in B£ from their customers. However, they can also exchange it for £ Sterling if they wish to. output.text_basic:
The answer is not to invent new means of security, but to revert to something fundamental and ancient: your memory. For millennia, people safeguarded their assets without the need for keys, by relying on their powers of recollection.

So why not do the same today? After all, it's possible to develop a photographic memory. Moreover, there are methods which, while not providing perfect recall, can dramatically improve a person's memory. For example:

1. The "method of loci" involves associating the items to remember with specific familiar locations. Walking through those locations in your mind, you'll recall the associated items.

2. The "memory palace" technique is also known as the "method of places." Similar in effect to the "method of loci," it involves "placing" the items to remember in a "palace" you know well, like your home.

3. The "peg system" involves assigning numbers or playing cards to "peg" items to, which are easier to remember. For example, "one" might correspond to "gun." So to remember something on your grocery list -- tomatoes -- conjure up an image of a gun shooting out tomatoes.

4. The "memory journey" technique involves placing objects along an imaginary journey through a familiar place. Each object will trigger a memory containing the information you need to recall.

While these techniques may seem cumbersome, each is well-suited to different types of memory tasks, and all can be surprisingly effective. Those with outstanding memories use these techniques intuitively, but they can be learnt by all.

Moreover, some scientists claim that mnemonics engage the brain's visual memory, sensory memory and long-term memory in a way that can actually improve overall brain function. So, beyond the practical benefits of remembering that one crucial thing, you're giving your brain a good workout.

Would you still worry about forgetting your password if you had a photographic memory? Probably not. But until then, how about trying one of these techniques for safeguarding those all-important keys to personal data? Your memory is the original keychain -- the only difference is that the keys are all safely stored in your head.

Let's look at the lifecycle of a plastic bottle and how recycling can help.

Lifecycle of a Plastic Bottle

When a new plastic bottle makes it to a recycling center, it goes through a wash to remove labels and contamination, is broken down into tiny pieces, and is melted into pellets.

Then it's shipped to a manufacturing company where it can be used to make new bottles or other products like clothing, carpeting, or playground toys.

What about other types of materials? Here's a glance at what happens to other common recyclables:

Aluminum Cans

Cans are recycled by shredding into small pieces, washing, and melting to form ingots (long bar-shaped pieces of metal) which are rolled into thin sheets that are used to make new cans.

Tin Cans and Steel Products

Tin cans are often made from steel with a thin layer of tin. Steel is shredded, melted down, and turned into new steel products. Tin is usually recycled by melting and reforming.

Paper Products

Paper products like newspapers are mixed with water to form a pulp that's strained and washed, then spread out on large screens, pressed and dried to make new paper products.

Recycling Saves Energy

The amount of energy saved by recycling one aluminum can is enough to run a TV set for three hours

Clouds are formed by the condensation of water vapor around tiny particles in the atmosphere. If there were no more clouds, there would be no cloud particles for water vapor to condense on, meaning no new clouds could form. 

Without clouds, the atmosphere would lack a key process for condensation, which is crucial for forming precipitation like rain and snow. Here's how the sequence would unfold:

1. **No Cloud Formation:** Without clouds, water vapor simply remains as a gas in the atmosphere. It doesn’t condense into liquid droplets.

2. **No Precipitation:** Since there are no cloud particles for condensation, precipitation processes like rain and snow cannot occur. The water vapor remains as a gas in the atmosphere.

3. **No Weather Patterns from Clouds:** Clouds play a significant role in weather patterns through their interactions with the Earth's surface and atmosphere. For instance, cumulus clouds indicate fair weather, while nimbostratus clouds often precede prolonged rain. Without clouds, these indicators would be absent, making weather prediction based on cloud formations impossible.

4. **Reliance on Other Factors:** Weather prediction would then need to rely solely on other atmospheric parameters, such as temperature, humidity, air pressure, and wind patterns. These factors can still provide insight into weather conditions but would lack the immediate visual and dynamic indicators that clouds presently provide.

5. **Potential for Increased Global Warming Effects:** Clouds also play a role in reflecting sunlight back into space (albedo effect), helping to cool the Earth. In the absence of clouds, more sunlight would reach the Earth's surface, potentially leading to increased surface warming and contributing to climate change.

In conclusion, without clouds, weather prediction would become more indirect and reliant on other atmospheric parameters. The lack of precipitation processes and changes in the Earth’s energy balance could introduce new complexities into forecasting and climate studies.

Square foot gardening is a simple way to create an efficient vegetable or flower garden. It fits into any space and is adaptable to almost any location. You plant each different crop in a different square according to the needs of each plant type. I will explain more about that a little later.

As a parent of a young child, I often wonder how children played before today’s myriad of plastic playthings. Were children of the past more resourceful and creative? Were they happier? Did they engage in more social play?

We have so many toys and gadgets and games today it seems overwhelming. It’s hard to keep them all organized and to keep track of them in our busy lives.  Are we short-changing our children when we give them these toys? Does simplicity lead to greater happiness and creativity?

Let’s take a look at history and see how children played before the abundance of today’s toys.

Early Childhood Toys and Play

There’s evidence that children have been playing with toys since the dawn of time. Researchers have discovered small figurines and carved balls from the prehistoric era.

In ancient Egypt, children played with dolls, marbles, balls, and a game called Senet that was played for fun and in ritual. In ancient Rome, children had dolls, lead military figures, hoops, masks, hobby horses, rattles, and balls. They also played a game similar to Tic Tac Toe.

Children in Medieval Europe played with marbles, hobby horses, tops, and rag dolls. They also played in the streets and fields with games like blind man’s bluff and leapfrog.

Children before the advent of modern toys had to use their imagination.

The Great Leap Forward In Toy Making

Childhood as we understand it today didn’t exist until the late 18th and early 19th centuries. Prior to the industrial revolution, many children left home to work or they were expected to work alongside adults. If children did have playtime, it was often unstructured and involved free play with nature and homemade objects.

The early 19th century marked a big change in the child-rearing philosophy in both Britain and America. It was thought that play was necessary for a child’s development and adults began to provide playthings. The toy industry as we understand it today was born.

The Growth of the American Toy Industry

The American toy industry thrived during the Industrial Revolution in the mid-19th century. Toy production moved from a cottage industry to factories which enabled cheaper and more consistent production.

During the 19th century and the early 20th century, dolls became a popular toy for girls. Rag dolls and dollhouses were especially popular. Boys had toy soldiers, toy guns, and various animal-themed toys such as rocking horses and toy dogs.

Would you learn a new skill like knitting or painting? Would you write a book or journal your thoughts? Whatever it may be, silence would afford you the opportunity to do it all without interruption, distraction, or disruption. For many, silence is a luxury that is difficult to come by. Between TV, radio, phones, and the constant chatter of family members or co-workers, sometimes a person just needs a moment of peace.

Silence is not only a luxury, but it is also a necessary element for human health. While many may think that silence simply means the absence of external noise, that is only part of the equation. True silence means a break from both exterior and interior noise. Here are four ways that real silence, which includes a break from internal noise, can be positively transformational.

Decreased Stress and Elevated Mood

Studies, such as one published in the journal Heart, found that two minutes of silence can be better for relaxation than listening to “relaxing” music. Another study out of the University of Manchester found that 15 minutes of walking meditation (a practice that can be silent or involve soothing sounds) in a quiet environment reduced symptoms of depression more than walking in a busy urban environment.

Better Concentration and Memory

Silence is also good for the brain. Research by Luciano Bernardi of the University of Pavia in Italy found that the brain can process information better in silence, leading to improved concentration and better memory retention. Even just taking a few quiet, reflective moments alone each day can help refresh the brain and improve mental functioning.

Enhanced Empathy and Introspection

In the absence of noise, it is more possible to tune into and understand the unspoken emotions and communications of others. Silence also provides a better opportunity for individuals to reflect on their personal thoughts, emotions, and beliefs. This can lead to a greater sense of purpose and personal autonomy.

Physical Healing

Finally, silence creates opportunities for the body to repair and heal itself. During silence, the parasympathetic nervous system takes over, leading to slower breathing, reduced heart rate, and lower blood pressure. This activation of the parasympathetic nervous system can promote healing and overall well-being.

While the modern world does not always allow for ample silence, it is important to make room for quiet reflection each day. This can range from a five-minute meditation break at work to a weekend retreat in the woods. Regardless of how it is incorporated, silence can be a powerful tool for enhancing health and well-being in many ways.

1. Review Your Meds

Some medications can make you sleepy or dizzy, which, in turn, can lead to falls. Review your medications and talk to your doctor about them, especially if you notice your balance or alertness is less than usual.

2. Get Your Vision Checked

If your eyeglasses are old or outdated, your eyesight may not be as sharp as it needs to be. Regular eye exams can help ensure you have glasses that best help your eyesight.

  • Remove scatter rugs, especially in hallways,

  • Use non-slip mats in your tub and shower,
  • Repair any cracks in your steps or walkways.

5. Seek Support

If you are having balance problems, consider seeking the guidance of a physical therapist. For people who experience falls or fear falling, Falls Prevention Programs or Therapeutic Exercise programs are very effective.

6. Wear Proper Footwear

Never walk around your home in your socks or stocking feet. Shoes provide traction and grip when you walk. If you wear shoes inside your home, consider slippers that have rubber grips on the bottom, and non-skid soles.

7. Carry a Medical Alert Device

In the event you do experience a fall, a medical alert device can help you get assistance as quickly as possible. You can talk directly to a care operator, or press the button for help to call 911.

Most people might answer, “I’d take a shower,” but what comes out of your showerhead? In many U.S. cities, the answer as recently as the 1970s was “not much other than water.” The water was clean enough but not optimally healthy for your skin, which is your body’s largest organ.

By the early 80s, people realized that adding minerals back into water could improve its healthful properties. It’s from this insight that mineral spring water was born.

If you’ve ever taken a swim in a mineral spring creek, you can attest to the refreshing and invigorating quality of mineral-rich water. It leaves your skin feeling silky smooth, and your hair shiny and bouncy.

Mineral spring waters contain naturally occurring dissolved minerals, including sulfate, magnesium, and calcium. These serve multiple functions, including aiding in digestion and helping cells send and receive messages.

Water companies capture spring water at its source, then filter out any impurities before bottling it as is. Because spring water is drawn directly from an underground cavity, it’s naturally filtered and contains unique minerals that are beneficial to your skin and hair.

Though tap water is usually safe to drink, it sometimes contains unwanted substances, such as chlorine, chloramine, and fluoride, that can dry out and damage your skin and hair.

Mineral spring water, on the other hand, replenishes moisture and leaves your skin nourished and your hair vibrant. Because it’s a natural source of magnesium, spring water also promotes relaxation and improves sleep quality.

Drinking enough water daily is crucial for maintaining good health. But with mineral spring water, you get all of these benefits and more.

And, more generally, why isn't there more technology advancement in transportation methods? Seems like everyone is just making slight modifications to existing models.


Transportation technology is advancing, but the rate of change is slower than in other areas

Technology advancement isn't just about the speed of change but also the ability to bring about practical improvements. In many cases, improvements to transportation have diminishing returns, where the increase in functionality or efficiency doesn't merit the cost, effort, and potential disruption to infrastructure.

  • Safety
    Automobiles are already among the safest modes of transportation. Future improvements will help, but there are limits to how safe they can be made before the restrictions imposed on driving and the increased cost price them out of the market.

  • Practicality
    The vast majority of transportation needs can already be met within the current technological landscape. For a new technology to have significant impact, it must provide meaningful benefits over what already exists – it must be significantly faster, safer, cheaper, more flexible, or any combination thereof. While concepts like flying cars and teleportation attract plenty of interest, they face significant challenges in practicability.

  • Infrastructure
    Much of our existing transportation infrastructure is built to support existing modes of transport. Changing this infrastructure is not only expensive but can cause significant disruptions to daily life. Consider the challenge of simply switching the US interstate highway system to magnetic levitation trains – every road would lose its purpose, necessitating the creation of a new transportation system for a vast number of shorter-distance trips, and the country would effectively grind to a halt while the transition happened.

  • The human element
    Many of the changes needed are psychological more than technological. People are accustomed to certain forms of travel, and they're comfortable with them. Convincing the public to adopt new forms of travel can take a lot of time and effort, and some changes may simply never catch on due to inconvenience or other issues. For example, many technologies are available to facilitate more efficient shared transit systems, but significant psychological and logistical barriers must be overcome before such systems can be widely adopted.

In short: our transportation system meets our needs pretty well as it is, and making major changes is difficult, expensive, and potentially very disruptive.

The idea is to reduce single-use plastic and consider a plastic-free lifestyle. But, if all plastic disappeared, would it be for the better? And if so, which materials could replace plastic?

It’s not all bad news for plastic. Like every material, both synthetic and natural, there are both negative and positive aspects. Plastic is versatile, cheap and durable. Its characteristics make it suitable for many applications. 

On the downside, the problem lies with single-use plastic. This includes plastic packaging, throwaway utensils and bags, the so-called disposable plastic items. A plastic-free lifestyle would look into more sustainable packaging options like paper. Paper can be recycled and it biodegrades easily. But, producing virgin paper from trees damages the forests. While plastics can be recycled, the recycling process is limited. Only a small amount of the plastic waste gets recycled due to technological constraints and high costs. Nevertheless, it's still important to keep recycling because every bit helps.

Well, one way to collect water is to condensate it out of the air. You've seen this happen on a cold bottle when you take it out of the fridge - water droplets form on the sides. You could make a bigger version of this using coils of pipe, and this is called a "condensing water generator".
In a desert you have 2 important sources of humid air: overnight air that has been cooled by the loss of heat into space, and the air in your breathing spaces (like your tent or bunker) that has been humidified by your own breathing and sweat.
To extract water from air, you need this air to cool down so it reaches its dew point and water droplets form. So a condensing water generator uses a heat exchanger to cool the air down enough for this to happen. Here are the components:

Cold coil (Condenser) - This is the pipe where cold air is blown. Because it's cold, any moisture in the air (humidity) condenses on it. This becomes water droplets, which run down the pipe and collect at the bottom.

Hot coil (Evaporator) - This is also a pipe, but hot air is blown through it. This causes any condensed water to evaporate, thus warming the pipe and losing heat energy so the air is nicely chilled when it reaches the cold coil.

A fluid circuit - This is something that carries heat from the hot side of the device to the cold side (and vice-versa). This could be water or refrigerant gas.

Now you have all the parts of a condensing water generator. Here's how you would assemble them:

Start by connecting the hot and cold coils in a loop, with the fluid circuit passing through both of them. For example, if you're using a refrigerant gas like ammonia, you would allow it to evaporate in the evaporator, which makes it very cold. It would then flow to the condenser, where it would release heat and condense back into liquid form.

Next, you'd attach a fan to blow air through the system. Air would pass through the hot coil first to heat the gas/refrigerant, cool down, then pass through the cold coil where it would hopefully condensate. The droplets would then run down the cold coil and be collected.

And that's it! You now have a system to condense water out of the air. Let's not forget to mention that this is actually exactly how your fridge works: to keep your food cool,

You probably couldn't rely on pain to caution you against dangerously hot surfaces or biting down on your tongue.

When you're injured or sense possible danger, your body experiences a cascade of biological reactions that ready you to fight or flee. Your heart beats faster to pump blood to your muscles for physical exertion. Your blood vessels dilate to improve your muscles' oxygen delivery. Your sweat increases to cool your skin. Your pupils dilate to improve long-distance vision. These changes, collectively referred to as the stress response or fight-or-flight response, involve the activation of your sympathetic nervous system. This system includes a network of nerves that extend throughout your body and influence your organs and other tissues.

Your body also communicates information about the state of your organs and tissues through your nerves. Sensory neurons, for instance, detect touch, temperature, pressure and pain throughout your body and relay that information to your brain so it has a current picture of what's happening.

This network relies heavily on the neurotransmitter norepinephrine to transmit messages. When released by neurons, norepinephrine adheres to receptors on a neighboring cell to continue the electrical signal down the line, or it causes metabolic changes in the cell that make the cell more excitable.

Your body's release of norepinephrine during the fight-or-flight response amplifies the information in those signals. It increases your blood pressure by causing your blood vessels to constrict and may trigger the breakdown of lipids into free fatty acids, which can provide energy during those times of stress.

But what happens when this system doesn't work correctly? We'll look at some of these disorders in the next section.­


Medical Disorders of the Sympathetic Nervous System



Adrenal Insufficiency



Horner's Syndrome



Frostbite or Hypothermia





Migraine Headaches





Raynaud's Phenomenon




Sympathetic Nervous System Facts

The part of your nervous system that mobilizes your response to stressful or dangerous situations isn't always welcome. Although it equips you to handle emergencies and acute stress, the sympathetic response has drawbacks in the modern world.

Chronic Stress: When faced with acute stress -- for example, physical danger or a short-term stressful situation -- your sympathetic nervous system response is adaptive and healthy. However, chronic stress can keep your sympathetic nervous system continually activated, which can harm your health. Chronic stress has been linked to increased risk for high blood pressure and heart disease. It also can contribute to problems like difficulties with sleep

What would you miss most? Let's find the answers.

Sand is a key element of the ecosystem. This ecosystem consists of the biological community (all plants, animals, and organisms) as well as their physical environment—such as the soil and rocks. Sand plays a major role in that environment by influencing air and water temperatures. Without a sandy beach, the shore would be significantly changed.

Firstly, the disappearance of sand would mean the absence of sand dunes. Dunes absorb energy from waves and wind, protecting the land. They also act as a reservoir, storing water that replenishes coastal vegetation and prevents it from drying out. Without sand dunes, the coastline would have little to no protection against storms, erosion, or rising sea levels. Moreover, inland areas would be at a higher risk of flooding and saltwater intrusion, contaminating water supplies.

As for changes in the biological community, some species depend on the sandy environment to breed, survive, or feed. Losing the sand would negatively affect creatures like sandpipers, crabs, and sand dollars, forcing them to relocate if possible. Even plants with deep root systems would struggle to thrive without the unique nutrient-rich sandy soil.

Beachfront vegetation, usually consisting of plants adapted to salty, windy conditions, would disappear. This vegetation serves as habitat and food sources for various animals, including insects, birds, and marine creatures. Consequently, the food chain would be disrupted, impacting the entire ecosystem.

Additionally, the aesthetics and recreational value of the beach would be significantly different. Swimmers, sunbathers, surfers, and beachgoers flock to sandy shores for the unique experience of walking on warm sand, listening to the sound of waves gently lapping the shore, and diving into the cool water. Without fine-grained sand, the beach would instead consist of larger pebbles, rocks, or possibly even concrete surfaces. This would fundamentally change the tactile, visual, and auditory experiences that draw people to beaches around the world.

Tourism, a vital sector of many economies, would take a hit. Beach towns and coastal communities rely on the sandy beach as a draw for tourists, which in turn supports local businesses from hotels to souvenir shops. Without sand, the coastal tourism industry would experience severe disruption, potentially leading to economic hardship for those communities.

To sum up, the absence of sand would deeply impact the biological community, tourism, and the ecosystem as a whole. The beach as we know it would be lost, affecting everything from climate protection to local economies and nature itself.

If everything became flat and textureless, how would you grasp their three-dimensionality? This is what people with agnosia face on a daily basis. The term, agnosia comes from the Greek words "a," meaning "without" and "gnosis," meaning "knowledge." Thus, it literally stands for "without knowledge." Agnosia refers to a range of cognitive disorders that compromise the ability to recognize objects, sounds, people, shapes, colors, or smells.

Agnosia can be caused by damage to various parts of the brain typically involving the occipital, parietal, or temporal regions. It is usually due to a stroke, traumatic brain injury, or neurodegenerative disorder such as Alzheimer’s disease. Depending on the region of the brain affected, agnosia takes different forms:

Visual agnosia occurs because of damage to the visual areas of the brain and impairs the person's ability to recognize visual stimuli. This includes inability to recognize familiar faces (prosopagnosia), inability to recognize objects (object agnosia), inability to determine the movement of objects (motion agnosia), or inability to recognize colors (color agnosia).

Auditory agnosia results from damage to the auditory processing areas of the brain and impairs the ability to recognize familiar sounds or voices, or differentiate between different sounds.

Tactile agnosia is caused by damage to the parietal lobe and impedes the patient's ability to understand and recognize tactile information.

Olfactory agnosia occurs due to damage to parts of the brain's smell processors and diminishes the ability to recognize smells.

Gustatory agnosia, which results from damage to the taste processing areas, impairs the ability to recognize flavors.

Associative agnosia is more complex and involves difficulty in recognizing familiar objects or faces when visual memory is impaired.

Agnosia underscores the critical importance of specific brain regions for perception and recognition that are largely interrelated. It also highlights how a breakdown in certain pathways can lead to severe disturbances in everyday life. Management options for agnosia typically depend on treating the underlying cause and may involve cognitive therapy, sensory substitution devices, and speech therapy. Researchers continue to explore advanced rehabilitation strategies and interventions that could potentially help agnosia patients recover their perceptual abilities.

Think of different methods and tools you could use to distinguish colors or objects when visual cues are absent.

1. **Sensory Touch**: You could use tactile differences. Objects have different textures and temperatures. Running your hands across surfaces can help differentiate materials like metal, plastic, wood, cloth, etc.
2. **Sound**: Different objects make different sounds when tapped, struck, or shaken. This auditory distinction can be useful.
3. **Smell**: Each object or material may have a unique odor. For example, rubber and leather smell distinctly different.
4. **Taste**: While not practical for most objects, for food and certain consumables, taste would be a distinguishing factor.
5. **Memory and Context**: Remembering what colors things usually are and using the context in which objects are found can help identify them.
6. **UV Light**: Some substances react to ultraviolet light differently and may fluoresce, helping differentiate them.
7. **Chemical indicators**: Certain chemicals can react with specific materials to produce different reactions or colors temporarily (thought this involves introducing color in a different manner).
8. **X-ray or MRI scans**: While not practical for everyday use, such technology can differentiate materials based on density and makeup.
9. **Electrical conductivity**: Using an electric tester to determine if objects are conductive or insulative could provide a basic differentiation.
10. **Reflectivity and Shine**: Objects reflect light differently, which could be discerned in absolute darkness by physical touch or through indirect means like detecting heat radiating off more insulating materials.
11. **Biological indicators**: Some animals or insects might be able to distinguish between objects based on pheromones or other chemical signals.
12. **Magnetic resonance**: Differences in material composition can sometimes be detected with magnetic resonance imaging or similar technology.
13. **Chemical reactions**: Spraying substances that react differently on contact with common materials can indicate what objects are made of.

In a world without colors, you would rely on contrast, textures, shapes, and other attributes to differentiate.

Here are six ways you might identify and distinguish objects despite their uniform colorlessness:

1. **Shape and Silhouette:**
   Different shapes help in distinguishing objects, even without colors. For example, a sphere won't look like a cube, and a tree won’t resemble a person, purely based on their shapes.

2. **Texture:**
   You could feel the texture of objects to tell them apart. Sandpaper would feel rough and a velvet cloth would feel smooth.

3. **Size:**
   Objects of different sizes can be told apart. A small keychain wouldn’t be confused with a large car.

4. **Shadow and Light Patterns:**
   The way light falls on objects can create different patterns, which help in identification. For example, the shadows cast by fingers on a wall.

5. **Reflection and Transparency:**
   In a colorless world, the way light reflects off an object (like a shiny metal surface) and its transparency (like a clear glass) can still be observed.

6. **Motion and Behavior:**
   Understanding an object's properties through its movement and behavior is also crucial. Liquid moves differently from a solid, and living vs. non-living objects behave differently.

So, while color does make it easier to quickly understand and interact with objects, removing color doesn't completely inhibit our ability to distinguish and identify them. Other sensory inputs and physical attributes still play critical roles in our perception of the world.

Text: According to the World Health Organization, air quality monitoring for PM2.5 (the most dangerous form of air pollution, that from ultrafine particles, 2.5 micrometers in diameter or less) has improved in 81 percent of countries over the last 15 years. WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus declared the situation a “silent public health emergency”: Outdoor air pollution now causes more diseases than well-known health threats like HIV/AIDS, diabetes or malaria. Exposure to air pollution is linked to lung cancer, strokes and heart disease, and it even kills crops and reduces agricultural yields. But it probably has some benefits, no? At least it can make great sunsets. Particles in the air scatter short wavelengths of light (blues and purples) more than longer wavelengths (oranges and reds). The higher the concentration of particles in the atmosphere, the more vivid the resulting sunsets. If you look out over New York or Beijing and see a fiery horizon, you can infer that air pollution is particularly bad there. Or go back to the days when large volcanoes like Pinatubo or Krakatoa erupted, throwing so much dust into the air that entire sunsets turned blood red. The flip side of this phenomenon is called “global dimming”, when particles in the air bounce incoming sunlight back into space, cooling the planet. This is thought to be the reason that temperatures didn’t rise as quickly in the 1950s and 1960s, a period marked by lots of dirty industry. In other words, air pollution could be acting as a brake on global warming. It sounds paradoxical: Pollution can warm the planet and cool it at the same time. But as scientists’ understanding of these processes grows, they’re figuring out just how complicated the relationship is between air pollution and climate change
